turns.speaker: cubbie
turns.text: Welcome back! Today we are tackling your tricky topic, the normal distribution.

turns.speaker: rival
turns.text: Why is it so special? It is just a lumpy hill!

turns.speaker: cubbie
turns.text: It is a continuous distribution, and actually the most important one of all, though it gets widely abused. You see it in psychology, business, and nursing.

turns.speaker: rival
turns.text: Wait, why does everything turn into a bell? Even shoe sizes?

turns.speaker: cubbie
turns.text: If you ask enough people about their shoe size, your graphed data really is bell-shaped! The curve is symmetric around the mean, so the mean equals the median.

turns.speaker: rival
turns.text: [sighs] Okay, but what controls how it looks? Can I squish it?

turns.speaker: cubbie
turns.text: The normal distribution depends only on the mean and standard deviation. Because the area under the curve must equal one, changing the standard deviation makes it fatter or skinnier.

turns.speaker: rival
turns.text: And what happens if I change the mean instead?

turns.speaker: cubbie
turns.text: [laughs] That just shifts the graph to the left or right! Because of that, there are an infinite number of normal probability distributions.

turns.speaker: rival
turns.text: Infinite curves sounds like a nightmare. How do you find where values fall?

turns.speaker: cubbie
turns.text: You use the Empirical Rule! About 68% of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean, about 95% within two, and about 99.7% within three.

turns.speaker: rival
turns.text: So almost all values lie within three standard deviations. Not bad for a lumpy hill.
